title: Loading: HttpClient, .Result and atomicity
sub: The game freezes, sockets run out, data drifts apart
cards/0/title: Story: three complaints about one button
cards/0/body:
The "Load model" button calls Load(url). QA files three tickets:

1. While the model loads, the game freezes.
2. After frequent reloads, connection errors pour in.
3. Loading the same model again throws ArgumentException, and search finds elements that are missing from the dictionary.

All three live in nine lines of one method.
cards/1/title: HttpClient is a phone exchange, not a call
cards/1/body:
HttpClient is meant to be an exchange you set up once and call through many times: inside it has a connection pool and reuses sockets that are already open.

A new HttpClient per call is a new exchange with its own pool. Old connections are not reused, and closed ones linger for minutes in TIME_WAIT. With frequent calls you run out of local ports: SocketException, even though the network is fine.
cards/1/deep: Here the old client is not even disposed: its connections close only when its finalizer runs, whenever the GC gets to it. But using (var c = new HttpClient()) per request is no cure either: the sockets still go to TIME_WAIT. The right way is one long-lived instance (static) or IHttpClientFactory. In modern .NET a long-lived client has its own trap: it does not notice DNS changes; SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime fixes that. In Unity, networking is often written with UnityWebRequest; on WebGL HttpClient does not work at all (no sockets).
cards/2/q: Load is called every couple of seconds. What will the line _http = new HttpClient() eventually cause?
cards/2/options/0: Sockets pile up, and new connections start failing with SocketException
cards/2/options/1: Nothing: HttpClient is a lightweight object with no resources
cards/2/options/2: A compiler warning that stops the build
cards/2/explain: Each client opens its own connections and does not share them. Closed connections keep the port in TIME_WAIT for a while. Under load this is port exhaustion, a classic .NET mistake.
cards/2/wrong/1: Inside HttpClient there is a handler with a connection pool and OS sockets. It is a heavy object.
cards/2/wrong/2: The compiler notices nothing here. The failure only shows up at runtime, under load.
cards/3/title: .Result: standing at the door until the parcel arrives
cards/3/body:
GetStringAsync is a delivery order: it immediately returns a "receipt" (a Task). .Result means "I will stand at the door doing nothing until it arrives". If the one standing is Unity's main thread, the whole game freezes: no frames, no input.

The second problem: the error does not arrive as is but wrapped in AggregateException, and catch (HttpRequestException) will not catch it.
cards/3/deep: HttpClient itself uses ConfigureAwait(false) internally, so this exact line usually "only" freezes the thread for the duration of the request. But wrap the call in your own async method without ConfigureAwait(false), call .Result on it from the main thread, and you get the classic deadlock: the continuation waits for the main thread through Unity's SynchronizationContext, and the main thread waits for the continuation. .GetAwaiter().GetResult() does not wrap the exception in AggregateException, but it blocks just the same, so it is not a fix.
cards/4/q: The server returned 404. Which exception reaches the caller of Load?
cards/4/options/2: None: Result returns an empty string
cards/4/explain: Task.Result wraps the task error in AggregateException. The real cause is in InnerException. With await you would get the original HttpRequestException.
cards/4/wrong/1: That is what await would give you. The blocking .Result wraps the exception.
cards/4/wrong/2: GetStringAsync checks the status code and fails the task for 404.
cards/5/task: The fields and the load method of ModelManager. Find the bugs: network, blocking, JSON data, atomicity and the key type.
cards/5/bugs/0/why: Every int Id is boxed on insert and on every lookup: extra allocations. Type safety is gone too: store a long and you will not find it by int.
cards/5/bugs/1/title: A new HttpClient on every call
cards/5/bugs/1/why: Each client starts its own connection pool, and the old one is never released. With frequent loads, sockets pile up and ports run out.
cards/5/bugs/2/why: The thread stands still during the request: on Unity's main thread the game freezes. Errors arrive in AggregateException, and there is no cancellation or timeout.
cards/5/bugs/3/why: For the JSON "null" or an empty response the result is null, and foreach throws NullReferenceException.
cards/5/bugs/4/why: The method clears nothing: a second call appends the same elements to _elements again.
cards/5/bugs/5/title: Add throws in the middle of the loop
cards/5/bugs/5/why: On a duplicate Id, Dictionary.Add throws ArgumentException. Some elements are already in _elements but not in _byId: the collections are out of sync.
cards/6/q: The model is already loaded. Load is called a second time with the same JSON. What happens? Select all.
cards/6/explain: The first element makes it into _elements, then _byId.Add on an existing Id throws ArgumentException and the loop stops. The list has N+1 elements, the dictionary has N. A "half-done" operation is exactly what a lack of atomicity looks like.
cards/7/title: Atomicity: pack a new box next to the old one
cards/7/body:
Do not move items one by one into a box people are already taking things from. Pack a new box next to it, check it, and only then swap it in for the old one in a single move.

Then any error (network, bad JSON, a duplicate Id) leaves the old data intact, and a repeated call creates no duplicates.
cards/7/deep: Swapping two fields (_elements = list; _byId = byId;) is atomic for a single thread. If readers live on other threads, they might see the new list with the old dictionary; then keep both in one immutable snapshot object and swap a single reference (Volatile.Write/Interlocked.Exchange). In Unity, the continuation after await returns to the main thread by default, so the swap happens where the data is read, and there is no race.
cards/8/q: Build a correct load: one client for the whole app and a dictionary without boxing.
cards/8/explain: One static readonly client reuses connections. Dictionary<int, ...> does not box keys. The new collections are built separately and swapped in only after every check, so an error never leaves the data "half loaded".
cards/9/title: object as a key: every number in its own box
cards/9/body:
To put an int where an object is expected, the runtime boxes the number into a box on the heap. Dictionary<object, ...> does this on every Add and every _byId[id]: garbage for the GC on every lookup.

It works: a boxed int is compared by value. But the compiler no longer checks the key type.
cards/9/code:
_byId.Add(5, e);           // the key is a boxed int
_byId.ContainsKey(5L);     // false: long 5 is not int 5
cards/9/deep: Int32.Equals(object) returns true only if the argument is also a boxed int; a boxed long or short with the same number is not equal. Dictionary<int, T> uses EqualityComparer<int>.Default, which works with int directly, without boxing. In Unity this shows up in the Profiler as GC Alloc in hot spots like the selection handler.
cards/10/q: What does the last line return?
cards/10/explain: The key is a boxed int 7, and the lookup uses a boxed short 7. These are different types, and Int32.Equals(object) returns false. With Dictionary<int, string>, the short would widen to int implicitly, and the lookup would succeed.
cards/10/wrong/1: The numbers are equal, but they are boxed as different types. For an object key, those are different keys.
cards/10/wrong/2: There is no cast here: the dictionary just compares objects with Equals.
cards/11/q: Put the steps of a reliable model reload in order.
cards/11/items/0: Download the JSON asynchronously with the shared HttpClient (with a cancellation token)
cards/11/items/1: Deserialize and replace null with an empty list
cards/11/items/2: Build a new dictionary, checking for duplicate Ids
cards/11/items/4: Notify subscribers that the model has been updated
cards/11/explain: Everything that can fail happens before the swap. Subscribers are called last, once the data is consistent.
cards/12/q: Match the line of Load with its problem.
cards/12/pairs/5/1: Boxing an int on every lookup
